Les amateurs de l’Amstel 65 cl se plaignent de sa carence dans la capitale, depuis début août. La Brarudi tranquilise.
L’Amstel 65cl se fait rare dans la capitale, observe les amoureux qui se sentent pénaliser par la Brarudi. Léonidas N., un habitué d’un snack bar du quartier Carama II, témoigne que cette pénurie a commencé à se manifester fin juillet. « Aujourd’hui, je me contente de l’Amstel 50 cl.» L’exportation de cette boisson en RDC pourrait être à l’ origine de cette pénurie.
«Pour avoir une Amstel 65 cl dans un bar de la capitale, il faut être un fidèle », raconte G.T. dans un bar du quartier Ngagara III. «Certains commerçants cachent le produit afin de le vendre à un prix très élevé.» Une bouteille s’achète à 2500Fbu dans certains bars alors que le prix officiel est de 1800Fbu. Cette pénurie oblige les consommateurs de cette bière à changer leurs habitudes. «Pourquoi la Brarudi nous prive de ce produit alors qu’il est disponible à l’intérieur du pays?» Et d’évoquer le projet de la Brarudi visant à harmoniser ses bouteilles avec celles en circulation dans la Communauté est-africaine.
M.A., un commerçant des produits Brarudi, confie que son fournisseur vend un casier d’Amstel à 26 000Fbu alors que le prix officiel est de 19 600Fbu. Ce qui l’oblige à vendre une bouteille d’Amstel 65 cl entre 2500 Fbu et 3000Fbu en fonction des affinités avec le client. Il révèle, en outre, ne pas servir tout le monde. «Cette pénurie est accentuée par certains commerçants qui exportent ce produit vers la RDC où il est très sollicité.» Et il exhorte la Brarudi à prendre des précautions pour que ces pénuries répétitives ne s’observent plus.
Quant aux grossistes de produits Brarudi, ils observent eux aussi cette pénurie. T. S., un de ces grossistes en zone Ngagara confie que cela fait deux semaines qu’il ne s’approvisionne pas en ce produit. «Ce dernier n’est pas disponible à la Brarudi.» Certains de ses clients ont annulé leurs commandes par manque de ce produit. Cette pénurie affecte considérablement son commerce. Il enregistre une perte de deux millions par semaine.
«Les boissons sont disponibles dans un format ou dans un autre»
Un communiqué de la Brarudi sorti le 1er a0ût précise que les boissons sont disponibles dans un format ou dans un autre. Elle constate une sensible hausse de la consommation de ses produits. Trois raisons majeures expliquent cette augmentation. La mauvaise récolte de bananes due au virus « Banana bunchy top » (une maladie qui a attaqué les plantations de bananes). Ceci a entraîné une carence de la bière traditionnelle et par conséquent un transfert de consommation vers des bières industrielles de Brarudi. La reprise de la fréquentation des bars, dont les propriétaires recommencent à investir dans le business. Et la reprise intense des cérémonies de fête. Cette relance de la consommation génère une utilisation accrue des emballages et par conséquent des casses de bouteilles et de caisses. Ce phénomène concerne toutes les marques de la Brarudi qui ne peuvent aujourd’hui être remplacées de façon optimale en raison du manque de devises que traverse le pays.
Afin de continuer à satisfaire les consommateurs, la Brarudi a mis en place un programme d’injection d’emballages 50 cl Amstel. «La chaîne de prix, de la Brarudi jusqu’au consommateur, en passant par les distributeurs reste inchangé.» Le communiqué précise, en outre, qu’il n’y a pas eu de changements majeurs au niveau des exportations des boissons Brarudi.
« Les consommateurs devraient jouir de leur droit à l’information »
Noël Nkurunziza, président de l’Association Burundaise des Consommateurs (Abuco), est catégorique : «Les consommateurs n’ont aucune information sur la situation actuelle. Or, leurs droits doivent être respectés. Ils devraient jouir du droit à l’information. »
Pour le président de l’Abuco, les raisons avancées par la Brarudi ne font qu’alimenter la spéculation tantôt sur le produit qui manque, tantôt sur le prix qui augmente. « Ce sont donc les consommateurs qui payent les coûts supplémentaires. »
M. Nkurunziza conseille à la Brarudi de sortir de son silence afin que les consommateurs puissent s’organiser en connaissance de cause. «La Brarudi ne produit pas pour elle-même, mais plutôt pour les consommateurs de ses produits.» Et il recommande à l’administration de faire respecter les prix officiels.
a2010.en:
Fans of the 65 cl Amstel are complaining about its scarcity in the capital since the start of August. Brarudi offers reassurance.

The 65 cl Amstel is becoming scarce in the capital, note the beer lovers who feel penalised by Brarudi. Leonidas N., a regular at a snack bar in the Carama II neighbourhood, testifies that this shortage began to show at the end of July. "Today I make do with the 50 cl Amstel." The export of this drink to the DRC could be the cause of the shortage.

"To get a 65 cl Amstel in a bar in the capital, you have to be a loyal customer," says G.T. in a bar in the Ngagara III neighbourhood. "Some traders hide the product in order to sell it at a very high price." A bottle sells for 2,500 Burundian francs in some bars, whereas the official price is 1,800 francs. This shortage is forcing consumers of this beer to change their habits. "Why does Brarudi deprive us of this product when it is available in the interior of the country?" And he points to Brarudi's plan to harmonise its bottles with those in circulation in the East African Community.

M.A., a trader in Brarudi products, confides that his supplier sells a crate of Amstel at 26,000 francs whereas the official price is 19,600 francs. This forces him to sell a 65 cl bottle of Amstel at between 2,500 and 3,000 francs depending on his relationship with the customer. He also reveals that he does not serve everyone. "This shortage is made worse by certain traders who export this product to the DRC, where it is much in demand." And he urges Brarudi to take precautions so that these repeated shortages no longer occur.

As for the wholesalers of Brarudi products, they too observe this shortage. T.S., one of these wholesalers in the Ngagara zone, confides that it has been two weeks since he was last supplied with this product. "It is not available at Brarudi." Some of his customers have cancelled their orders for lack of this product. This shortage considerably affects his business. He is recording a loss of two million per week.

"The drinks are available in one format or another"

A Brarudi press release issued on 1 August states that the drinks are available in one format or another. The company notes a marked rise in the consumption of its products. Three major reasons explain this increase. The poor banana harvest due to the "Banana bunchy top" virus (a disease that has attacked banana plantations). This has led to a shortage of traditional beer and consequently a shift in consumption towards Brarudi's industrial beers. The return of customers to bars, whose owners are starting to invest in the business again. And the intense resumption of festive ceremonies. This revival in consumption generates increased use of packaging and consequently breakages of bottles and crates. This phenomenon concerns all Brarudi brands, which today cannot be replaced optimally because of the shortage of foreign currency the country is going through.

In order to continue satisfying consumers, Brarudi has set up a programme to inject 50 cl Amstel packaging. "The price chain, from Brarudi to the consumer, via the distributors, remains unchanged." The press release further states that there have been no major changes in the export of Brarudi drinks.

"Consumers should enjoy their right to information"

Noel Nkurunziza, president of the Burundian Consumers' Association (Abuco), is categorical: "Consumers have no information on the current situation. Yet their rights must be respected. They should enjoy the right to information."

For the president of Abuco, the reasons put forward by Brarudi only fuel speculation, sometimes about the product that is missing, sometimes about the price that is rising. "So it is the consumers who pay the additional costs."

Mr Nkurunziza advises Brarudi to break its silence so that consumers can organise themselves in full knowledge of the facts. "Brarudi does not produce for itself, but rather for the consumers of its products." And he recommends that the administration enforce the official prices.

a2232.t:
Muktasari:
- Msongamano wa watu, magari umeongezeka kwenye mitaa ya Kariakoo kuelekea Sikukuu ya Eid, kwa akiasi kikubwa wanunuzi ni wanawake.
Dar es Salaam. Siku chache kabla ya waumini wa dini ya Kiislamu kusherehekea sikukuu ya Eid, mitaa ya Kariakoo imefurika watu leo Machi 29, 2025 waliofuata mahitaji mbalimbali.
Katika mitaa kumekuwa na msongamano wa watu, magari na bidhaa zilizopangwa kando mwa barabara, watoto wakijikuta katika hali ngumu.
Kwenye mitaa ya Msimbazi, Congo, Mkunguni, Sikukuu, Nyamwezi na Uhuru, baadhi ya wazazi na walezi waliofuatana na watoto wamekuwa wakipita kwenye maduka na vibanda kununua nguo na viatu.
Salma Hamisi, mama wa watoto wawili aliyetoka Mbagala wilayani Temeke, anasema: “Mwaka jana bei zilikuwa tofauti kabisa, tulinunua magauni ya watoto kwa Sh25,000 lakini sasa ni Sh30,000 na kuendelea. Viatu navyo vimepanda, lakini siwezi kuacha watoto wangu wakose furaha ya Eid,” amesema Salma akiwa ameshika mifuko miwili yenye mavazi aliyowanunulia watoto wake katika Mtaa wa Congo.
Miongoni mwa nguo zilizopanda bei ni abaya kwa ajili ya wanawake ambazo za kawaida ziliuzwa kuanzia Sh30,000 awali lakini kuanzia Machi 28, 2025 zinauzwa Sh35,000 hadi Sh60,000. Kwa zenye urembo na nakshi zaidi zikiuzwa hadi Sh130,000. Si kwa abaya pekee, bei zimepanda hata kwa madera na vijora.
“Huu ni wakati wa watoto, sisi wazazi tunaweza kuvaa za mwaka jana,” amesema Jamila Said, akiwa na watoto wake watatu wakichagua nguo katika Mtaa wa Narung’ombe.
Licha ya mvua kunyesha kuanzia alfajiri kabla ya kukatika baadaye mchana, eneo la Kariakoo kumekuwa na hali ya joto kutokana na msongamano.
Joto liliongezeka ndani ya maduka katika Mtaa wa Raha baada ya umeme kukatika tangu saa sita mchana.
Wengi walioonekana kwenye mitaa ya Kariakoo ni wanawake, baadhi wakiwa wamebeba watoto mgongoni, wengine wakishikwa mikono.
“Msongamano huu ni wa kila mwaka, lakini hatuna namna. Tunajua tutaumia na tutakanyagana, lakini tukifika nyumbani watoto wakivaa nguo mpya na kucheza kwa furaha, tunasahau tabu zote,” amesema Mohamed Rashid, baba wa watoto wawili aliyekuwa Mtaa wa Nyamwezi akinunua kanzu kwa ajili ya mtoto wake.
Wachuuzi nao wanapita huku na huko wakinadi bidhaa za nguo, viatu na mapambo.
"Haya twende kazi tuvae abaya na vijora bila kumsahau mwanao nguo Sh6,000 twende kazi mama penda mwanao akatambie wenziwe mtaani," ndivyo alivyonadi bidhaa Athumani Salehe, katika Mtaa wa Raha.
Katika msongamano huo, baadhi si wanunuzi wa bidhaa bali wamewasindikiza wenzao kununua mahitaji kama anavyoeleza Amina Sheria mfanyabiashara wa madera:
“Unakuta wameongezana wanne unawakaribisha wanachagua, anatokea mmoja anasema hiyo mbaya tuondoke, hawa wanatuharibia biashara badala ya kuacha mtu aamue wao wana kazi ya kuponda alichopenda mwenzao."
Mchuuzi wa nguo za kiume, Peter Selem amesema kwa upande wake biashara si nzuri.
"Wanaofika dukani ni wachache wateja ninaopata ni walewale wanaokuja kuchukua mzigo wa jumla na wanaotoka nje ya Tanzania tofauti na matarajio yangu nilijua nitaongeza wateja wapya kipindi hiki," amesema.
Maduka ya viungo
Katika maandalizi ya sikukuu, maduka yanayouza viungo kwenye Mtaa wa Tandamti na Sikukuu kumekuwa na umati.
"Nimekuja kununua viungo Karikaoo kwa sababu ni vizuri na si vya kukaa dukani muda mrefu, bei yake ni nafuu tofauti na masoko mengine ndiyo maana nipo hapa navumilia foleni ili nipate kilicho bora," amesema Hadija Seif, mkazi wa Upanga.
Msongamano wa magari
Barabara za Msimbazi na Uhuru zimekuwa na msongamano wa magari sawa na barabara ya Mafia, hivyo watu kulazimiaka kukaa barabarani kwa zaidi ya saa moja kabla ya kufika waendako.
Hali ikiwa hivyo, bodaboda na bajaji zimekuwa zikipenya kila zinapopata upenyo hivyo kuhatarisha usalama wa watu.
a2232.en:
Kariakoo floods ahead of the Eid holiday, abayas rise in price

Summary:
- The congestion of people and vehicles has increased in the streets of Kariakoo ahead of the Eid holiday, with the buyers largely being women.

Dar es Salaam. A few days before the Muslim faithful celebrate the Eid holiday, the streets of Kariakoo were flooded today, March 29, 2025, with people seeking various necessities.

In the streets there has been congestion of people, vehicles and goods laid out along the roadside, with children finding themselves in difficult conditions.

On Msimbazi, Congo, Mkunguni, Sikukuu, Nyamwezi and Uhuru streets, some parents and guardians accompanied by children have been going through shops and stalls buying clothes and shoes.

Salma Hamisi, a mother of two who came from Mbagala in Temeke district, says: "Last year the prices were completely different, we bought children's dresses for Sh25,000 but now it is Sh30,000 and above. Shoes have also gone up, but I cannot let my children miss the joy of Eid," said Salma while holding two bags with the clothes she had bought for her children on Congo Street.

Among the clothes whose prices have risen are abayas for women, which ordinarily sold from Sh30,000 previously but since March 28, 2025 are being sold at Sh35,000 up to Sh60,000. Those with more decoration and embroidery sell for up to Sh130,000. It is not for abayas alone; prices have also risen for maderas and vijora.

"This is the children's time; we parents can wear last year's clothes," said Jamila Said, who was with her three children choosing clothes on Narung'ombe Street.

Despite rain falling from dawn before stopping later in the afternoon, the Kariakoo area has been hot because of the congestion.

The heat increased inside the shops on Raha Street after the electricity went off from midday.

Most of those seen in the streets of Kariakoo are women, some carrying children on their backs, others holding them by the hand.

"This congestion happens every year, but we have no choice. We know we will suffer and be trampled on, but when we get home and the children wear new clothes and play happily, we forget all the hardship," said Mohamed Rashid, a father of two who was on Nyamwezi Street buying a kanzu for his child.

Hawkers move here and there advertising clothes, shoes and ornaments.

"Come on, let's go, let's wear abaya and vijora without forgetting your child's clothes at Sh6,000; let's go, mama, love your child so that he can boast to his friends in the neighbourhood," is how Athumani Salehe advertised his goods on Raha Street.

In that crowd, some are not buyers of goods but have accompanied others who are buying necessities, as explained by Amina Sheria, a trader in madera garments:

"You find that four of them have come together, you welcome them, they choose, then one of them says that one is bad, let's go; these people spoil our business instead of letting a person decide - they make it their job to run down whatever their companion liked."

A vendor of men's clothing, Peter Selem, said that for his part business is not good.

"Few people come to the shop; the customers I get are the same ones who come to take wholesale loads and those coming from outside Tanzania, contrary to my expectations - I thought I would gain new customers during this period," he said.

Spice shops

In preparation for the holiday, the shops selling spices on Tandamti and Sikukuu streets have had crowds.

"I have come to buy spices at Kariakoo because they are good and not ones that have sat in the shop a long time; the price is cheaper than at other markets, that is why I am here enduring the queue so that I get what is best," said Hadija Seif, a resident of Upanga.

Traffic congestion

Msimbazi and Uhuru roads have had traffic congestion, as has Mafia road, so people are forced to sit on the road for more than an hour before reaching their destinations.

With the situation like that, boda bodas and bajajis have been squeezing through wherever they find a gap, thereby endangering people's safety.

a2453.t:
Des milliers de familles ont été contraintes de fuir leurs foyers dans l’Etat du Darfour-Nord en raison de l’intensification des combats dans cette région de l’ouest du Soudan, a appris APA mercredi.
Entre le 30 et le 31 janvier 2025, près de 3 700 ménages ont été déplacés à la suite des combats dans la localité d’El Fasher, au Darfour-Nord, portant à plus de 605 000 le nombre total de personnes déplacées dans cette région depuis avril 2024, a annoncé l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM).
Les villages de Shagra A, Shagra B, Shagra C, Golo et Jouki ont été particulièrement touchés par les violences. Les déplacés ont cherché refuge dans d’autres zones de la localité d’El Fasher, où des incendies ont également été signalés, détruisant des biens personnels. La situation demeure incertaine et tendue, la localité étant assiégée par les paramilitaires des Forces de soutien rapide (FSR) depuis mai 2024.
Depuis le début du conflit en avril 2023 entre l’armée régulière et les FSR, plus de 12 millions de personnes ont été déplacées au Soudan, dont 8,8 millions à l’intérieur du pays et 3,3 millions qui ont fui vers des pays voisins. En dépit des efforts humanitaires, l’accès aux zones affectées reste limité, exacerbant la souffrance des populations.
L’OIM a également rapporté une forte augmentation des attaques et des déplacements dans d’autres localités du Darfour-Nord depuis octobre 2024, notamment à Kutum, Kebkabiya, Melit et Al Koma. De plus, des conflits intercommunautaires dans la localité de Dar As Salam ont ajouté à la crise, contribuant à près de 10 % des incidents signalés dans la région depuis avril 2024.
En réponse à la situation de plus en plus désastreuse, l’agence onusienne appelle la communauté internationale à renforcer ses efforts pour fournir une aide humanitaire urgente et soutenir les efforts visant à mettre fin à ce conflit dévastateur.
Le Bureau de coordination des affaires humanitaires de l’ONU (OCHA) a également exprimé des préoccupations majeures concernant la malnutrition sévère, notamment dans l’État de Khartoum, où plus de 70 décès, principalement chez les enfants, ont été liés à la faim. Les conditions de famine au camp de déplacés d’Abu Shouk près d’El Fasher, à la fin du mois de décembre 2024, ont particulièrement alarmé l’OCHA.
En plus de la crise alimentaire, des rapports d’arrestations et de harcèlement à l’encontre des déplacés internes se multiplient, notamment dans les régions du Darfour et à Khartoum. Le Haut-commissariat des Nations Unies pour les réfugiés (HCR) souligne les préoccupations croissantes en matière de protection, y compris l’augmentation des violences sexistes et les risques accrus pour les enfants.
Le HCR a également noté que les centres de transit au Soudan du Sud, destination de milliers de réfugiés soudanais, sont saturés à plus de 340 % de leur capacité. En janvier 2025, plus d’un million de personnes, incluant des réfugiés soudanais et des rapatriés sud-soudanais, ont franchi la frontière vers le Soudan du Sud, un pays déjà confronté à des défis humanitaires considérables.
ODL/te/Sf/APA
a2453.en:
Sudan: thousands of newly displaced people in North Darfur

Thousands of families have been forced to flee their homes in North Darfur State because of the intensification of fighting in that region of western Sudan, APA learned on Wednesday.

Between 30 and 31 January 2025, nearly 3,700 households were displaced following fighting in the locality of El Fasher, in North Darfur, bringing to more than 605,000 the total number of displaced people in that region since April 2024, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) announced.

The villages of Shagra A, Shagra B, Shagra C, Golo and Jouki were particularly affected by the violence. The displaced sought refuge in other areas of the El Fasher locality, where fires were also reported, destroying personal property. The situation remains uncertain and tense, the locality having been besieged by the paramilitaries of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since May 2024.

Since the start of the conflict in April 2023 between the regular army and the RSF, more than 12 million people have been displaced in Sudan, including 8.8 million inside the country and 3.3 million who have fled to neighbouring countries. Despite humanitarian efforts, access to the affected areas remains limited, exacerbating the suffering of the populations.

The IOM also reported a sharp increase in attacks and displacement in other localities of North Darfur since October 2024, notably in Kutum, Kebkabiya, Melit and Al Koma. In addition, intercommunal conflicts in the locality of Dar As Salam have added to the crisis, contributing to nearly 10% of the incidents reported in the region since April 2024.

In response to the increasingly disastrous situation, the UN agency calls on the international community to step up its efforts to provide urgent humanitarian aid and to support efforts aimed at ending this devastating conflict.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has also expressed major concerns about severe malnutrition, notably in Khartoum State, where more than 70 deaths, mainly among children, have been linked to hunger. The famine conditions at the Abu Shouk displacement camp near El Fasher, at the end of December 2024, particularly alarmed OCHA.

In addition to the food crisis, reports of arrests and harassment of internally displaced people are multiplying, notably in the Darfur regions and in Khartoum. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) highlights growing protection concerns, including the increase in gender-based violence and the heightened risks for children.

UNHCR also noted that the transit centres in South Sudan, the destination of thousands of Sudanese refugees, are saturated at more than 340% of their capacity. In January 2025, more than one million people, including Sudanese refugees and South Sudanese returnees, crossed the border into South Sudan, a country already facing considerable humanitarian challenges.

ODL/te/Sf/APA

a2493.t:
The United States Senate has moved to exempt the global anti-AIDS programme, President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), from major foreign aid cuts proposed by President Donald Trump’s administration.
This development offers hope to millions of people living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria and other developing countries.
The decision follows pressure from key Republican senators who resisted a White House-backed plan to slash $400 million from PEPFAR.
First launched in 2003 under President George W. Bush, the government says PEPFAR has provided life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support to more than 25 million people worldwide.
After a closed-door meeting on Tuesday with Senate Republicans, White House Office of Management and Budget Director, Russell Vought confirmed that the administration would support a substitute amendment that leaves PEPFAR funding intact, The Hill, an American newspaper, reports.
“There is a substitute amendment that does not include the PEPFAR rescission, and we’re fine with that,” Mr Vought told reporters, adding that the overall size of the spending cuts package would remain about $9 billion.
The amendment means the legislation must return to the House of Representatives for another round of voting before a Friday deadline.
Why it matters
In Nigeria and other developing countries, PEPFAR plays a critical role in the national HIV response, approximately funding up to 90 per cent of the country’s HIV treatment programmes.
The initiative has committed more than $6 billion to Nigeria, strengthening testing, treatment and health systems.
Public health officials and civil society groups had raised alarm over the proposed cuts, warning that any reduction could further put millions at risk of treatment interruption.
Just last month, a UNAIDS report warned that abrupt US aid withdrawals had already destabilised supply chains, forced the closure of some HIV treatment facilities, and left thousands of healthcare workers out of jobs in countries like South Africa.
It also warned that analysis suggests four million additional AIDS-related deaths between now and 2029, including 300,000 additional children’s deaths, if programmes permanently lose PEPFAR’s support.
In response to the US aid cuts, Nigeria’s National Assembly approved an additional N300 billion for the health sector in the 2025 budget.
The government also approved N4.8 billion for the procurement of 150,000 HIV treatment packs under the 2024/2025 HIV Programme Alignment and also announced plans to absorb health workers into the public health workforce.
Republican pushback
PREMIUM TIMES gathered that the move to exempt PEPFAR followed resistance from several Republican senators who argued that slashing the programme’s funding would undermine decades of progress in the global HIV/AIDS fight.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune was quoted by The Hill as saying he planned to hold two procedural votes on Tuesday to advance the package.
These include a motion to discharge the legislation from the Senate Appropriations Committee and another to move it forward on the Senate floor.
“Rescissions have been a part of the process around here for a long time, not only in the annual appropriations process,” Mr Thune said, noting that past presidents from both parties had submitted similar proposals to Congress.
He added that the current package represented only a fraction of the federal budget. “What we’re talking about here is one tenth of one per cent of all federal spending,” he added. “That’s one-thousandths of the federal budget that’s included in this rescissions package.”

a2540.t:
Le retour de Donald Trump à la Maison-Blanche en 2025 pourrait marquer un tournant pour le secteur énergétique africain. En relançant des financements bloqués sous l’administration Biden, sa politique ouvre la voie à une exploitation accrue des énergies fossiles sur le continent. Une opportunité stratégique ou un risque pour la transition énergétique ?
Le retour de Donald Trump à la Maison-Blanche en 2025 a relancé le débat sur l’avenir énergétique de l’Afrique. Certains analystes y voient une occasion unique pour le continent d’affirmer son potentiel en énergies fossiles.
La réapprobation rapide d’un prêt de 4,7 milliards de dollars par la Banque américaine d’import-export pour le projet de gaz naturel liquéfié (GNL) de TotalEnergies au Mozambique – bloqué sous l’administration Biden – donne le ton de ce qui pourrait être une transformation majeure pour le secteur énergétique africain.
Un changement de cap favorable aux énergies fossiles
NJ Ayuk, président exécutif de la Chambre africaine de l’énergie (AEC), estime que la politique énergétique de Trump représente une opportunité pour l’Afrique d’exploiter pleinement ses vastes ressources en hydrocarbures.
« L’Afrique doit saisir ce moment potentiellement bref de l’histoire et voir l’administration Trump comme un partenaire plutôt qu’un adversaire », affirme-t-il.
Selon lui, les pressions internationales en faveur des énergies vertes ont freiné l’industrialisation et la croissance économique du continent, qui restent fortement dépendantes des énergies fossiles.
« Trop longtemps, ces pressions ont poussé les pays africains à délaisser leurs ressources en combustibles fossiles au profit d’une transition énergétique qui ne correspond pas toujours à leurs besoins immédiats », ajoute-t-il.
L’action décisive de Trump sur le projet de GNL au Mozambique pourrait signaler un renouveau du partenariat énergétique entre les États-Unis et l’Afrique, en privilégiant le développement économique plutôt que les engagements idéologiques en faveur de la décarbonation.
Un modèle à suivre pour les pays africains ?
La relance de ce projet illustre comment la volonté politique peut accélérer les processus bureaucratiques et faciliter le financement d’initiatives énergétiques sur le continent. Ce virage contraste fortement avec la réticence de l’administration Biden à soutenir les nouveaux projets d’énergie fossile, perçue par de nombreux dirigeants africains comme un frein au développement économique.
Le slogan de Trump, « forer, forer, forer », bien que conçu dans sa logique « America First », pourrait inspirer les pays africains à adopter leur propre approche : « Afrique d’abord ». Ayuk encourage ainsi les gouvernements africains à soutenir tout projet prometteur d’exploration et de production pétrolière et gazière, en simplifiant les réglementations et en attirant les investissements étrangers.
Une opposition aux objectifs climatiques mondiaux ?
Les critiques soulignent que cette approche favorisant les combustibles fossiles entre en contradiction avec les engagements internationaux en matière de lutte contre le changement climatique. Cependant, l’AEC insiste sur le fait que la réalité africaine est différente : le continent ne représente qu’une fraction des émissions mondiales, mais souffre de manière disproportionnée de la précarité énergétique.
Dans ce contexte, le charbon, souvent décrié à l’échelle mondiale, pourrait offrir une solution accessible et efficace pour répondre aux besoins croissants en électricité. La volonté de Trump de défier l’opposition internationale à la production de charbon pourrait inciter certains pays africains à rouvrir leurs mines et exploiter leurs abondantes réserves.
L’Afrique du Sud, par exemple, pourrait jouer un rôle clé en développant des technologies de « charbon propre », conciliant accessibilité financière et préoccupations environnementales. D’autres pays disposant de réserves inexploitées pourraient suivre cet exemple afin de réduire leur dépendance à l’aide étrangère et renforcer leur souveraineté énergétique.
Un leadership africain nécessaire
Pour concrétiser cette vision, les gouvernements africains devront faire preuve d’un leadership audacieux en surmontant les obstacles réglementaires, les défis sécuritaires et le lobbying anti-carbone.
Comme le souligne Ayuk : « Les quatre prochaines années sous Trump pourraient redéfinir le paysage énergétique de l’Afrique. La question est de savoir si nos dirigeants auront le courage et la clairvoyance nécessaires pour en tirer parti. »
JN/fss/ac/APA
a2540.en:
Trump and Africa: an opportunity for fossil energy?
Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025 could mark a turning point for the African energy sector. By reviving financing that was blocked under the Biden administration, his policy opens the way to increased exploitation of fossil fuels on the continent. A strategic opportunity or a risk for the energy transition?
Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025 has revived the debate on Africa's energy future. Some analysts see it as a unique chance for the continent to assert its fossil energy potential.
The rapid re-approval of a $4.7 billion loan by the US Export-Import Bank for TotalEnergies' liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Mozambique - blocked under the Biden administration - sets the tone for what could be a major transformation for the African energy sector.
A change of course favourable to fossil fuels
NJ Ayuk, executive chairman of the African Energy Chamber (AEC), believes that Trump's energy policy represents an opportunity for Africa to fully exploit its vast hydrocarbon resources.
"Africa must seize this potentially brief moment in history and see the Trump administration as a partner rather than an adversary," he says.
According to him, international pressure in favour of green energy has held back the continent's industrialisation and economic growth, which remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels.
"For too long, these pressures have pushed African countries to abandon their fossil fuel resources in favour of an energy transition that does not always match their immediate needs," he adds.
Trump's decisive action on the LNG project in Mozambique could signal a revival of the energy partnership between the United States and Africa, prioritising economic development over ideological commitments to decarbonisation.
A model for African countries to follow?
The revival of this project illustrates how political will can accelerate bureaucratic processes and facilitate the financing of energy initiatives on the continent. This shift contrasts sharply with the Biden administration's reluctance to support new fossil energy projects, which many African leaders perceived as a brake on economic development.
Trump's slogan, "drill, drill, drill", although conceived within his "America First" logic, could inspire African countries to adopt their own approach: "Africa first". Ayuk thus encourages African governments to support any promising oil and gas exploration and production project, by simplifying regulations and attracting foreign investment.
Opposition to global climate goals?
Critics point out that this approach favouring fossil fuels contradicts international commitments on combating climate change. However, the AEC insists that the African reality is different: the continent accounts for only a fraction of global emissions, yet suffers disproportionately from energy poverty.
In this context, coal, often decried globally, could offer an accessible and effective solution to meet growing electricity needs. Trump's willingness to defy international opposition to coal production could encourage some African countries to reopen their mines and exploit their abundant reserves.
South Africa, for example, could play a key role by developing "clean coal" technologies, reconciling affordability and environmental concerns. Other countries with untapped reserves could follow this example in order to reduce their dependence on foreign aid and strengthen their energy sovereignty.
African leadership needed
To make this vision a reality, African governments will need to show bold leadership by overcoming regulatory obstacles, security challenges and anti-carbon lobbying.
As Ayuk stresses: "The next four years under Trump could redefine Africa's energy landscape. The question is whether our leaders will have the courage and foresight needed to take advantage of it."
JN/fss/ac/APA

a2717.t:
Government has downplayed the absence of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the G20 Foreign Minister Summit in Johannesburg which started on Thursday.
With the ongoing tensions between South Africa and the US, Rubio decided to boycott the summit after President Donald Trump signed an executive order withdrawing foreign aid, claiming that South Africa was expropriating land from white farmers without compensation under the new Expropriation Act.
Rubio was also against the theme of the summit - solidarity, equality and sustainability. He claimed that the country was not promoting equality because of the alleged land grabs.
However, South Africa's G20 sous sherpa, Xolisa Mabhongo, said the US would be represented by a senior diplomat, Dana Brown, at the summit, which starts at the Nasrec Expo Centre on Thursday. (South Africa has two sous sherpas, high-ranking officials who coordinate the G8 and G20 summits. The other one is Advocate Nokukhanya Jele.)
Mabhongo said:
He said all G20 countries are represented. Mabhongo said the G20 operates based on a troika consisting of South Africa, previous host Brazil and the US.
Part of those discussions include the road map towards the US presidency next year. "So, we do not foresee any problems in that," he added.
Responding to the City Press question about Rubio's disapproval of the theme, Mabhongo said the theme was approved by former US president Joe Biden's administration, whose term ended last month. He said the new Trump administration had raised issues because of false information.
Mabhongo said foreign ministers from 15 countries will attend, while four deputy ministers of foreign affairs will represent their nations.
"Only one country, the US, will be represented by a senior diplomat," he said.
For the first time in the history of the summit, which was founded in 1999 following the Asian financial crisis, it will be held on African soil.
The Asian financial crisis forced the developing and developed countries to form a forum for the finance ministers and central bank governors to discuss global economic and financial issues. It was later upgraded to the level of heads of state/government in the wake of the global economic and financial crisis of 2007 and 2009.
Since then, the G20 summit has been held annually under a rotating presidency. The G20 initially focused largely on broad macroeconomic issues, but it has since expanded its agenda to include trade, sustainable development, health, agriculture, energy, environment, climate change and anti-corruption. Among the G20 members are the US, the UK, France, Germany, India, Canada, China and Argentina.
The foreign minister's summit is expected to be attended by 35 countries, including the 20 permanent members.
Mabhongo said President Cyril Ramaphosa invited 15 other countries as guests to this year's summit. These include Spain, the Netherlands, Algeria, Egypt, Angola, the United Arab Emirates and Nigeria.
He said there has been an ongoing discussion between South Africa and the US with the hope to resolve the impasse. The summit will be officially opened by Ramaphosa and is expected to discuss the current global geopolitical situation and map the way forward.
The current differences between South Africa and the US were being handled by the troika of the summit, which includes Brazil. "This is the beginning of our presidency for the whole year - until the end of November. So, we are in conversations with the US," Mabhongo said.
He emphasised the importance of South Africa's role in the G20, adding that holding the presidency is significant for the country because it allows South Africa to present a development agenda on the G20.
He added:
Jele said the G20 carries tremendous responsibility because the decisions taken by the summit directly impact the lives of the global community.
"The world faces a myriad of global challenges and continues to suffer developmental reversals. The current global situation suggests that the international community requires a profound paradigm shift characterised by solidarity, harmony, and mutual respect. In this regard, the G20 has a significant role to play in fostering global cooperation and collaboration to address the challenges and achieve sustainable development," Jele said.

a2719.t:
British-Ghanaian singer Fuse ODG, who recently criticised foreign aid in Africa, has released a music video entitled We Know It’s Christmas, in a rebuttal to the 40th anniversary remake of Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas?
The singer/rapper said his latest track is "not just a song" but "a statement".
The video begins with the Grammy-winning star declaring live on ITV's Good Morning Britain programme that "African problems need to be solved by Africans".
It follows Ed Sheeran saying last month that Band Aid had not asked for permission to re-use his vocals from a 30th anniversary version of their track. He then credited Fuse ODG, who had declined the offer to take part in the project, for updating his view of the situation.
Sheeran said: "A decade on and my understanding of the narrative associated with this has changed, eloquently explained by @fuseodg".
Fuse ODG had posted: "I refused to participate in Band Aid because I recognised the harm initiatives like it inflict on Africa.
"While they may generate sympathy and donations, they perpetuate damaging stereotypes that stifle Africa's economic growth, tourism, and investment, ultimately costing the continent trillions and destroying its dignity, pride and identity."
Fuse ODG won a Grammy for his collaborative work on Sheeran's 2017 song Bibia Be Ye Ye. Now his own latest music video features beautiful waterfalls and bustling cities, as well as making nods to famous black leaders including former Ghana president Kwame Nkrumah.
Speaking about We Know It's Christmas (Band Aid Reply), the songwriter said it was intended as "a reflection of where we’ve come from and where we’re going".
"Ten years ago, I made a stand because I believed it was time for Africans to tell their own stories and to redefine the narrative," he said.
"This song is a celebration of that shift. We're no longer waiting for charity; we’re building our own futures," he added.
"This is about empowerment, pride, and showing the world that Africa’s story is far more than poverty and aid."
The release is an audiovisual response to the latest incarnation of Do They Know It's Christmas? - a charity song first written in 1984 by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure to raise money for the famine in Ethiopia.
The new "ultimate mix" of the Band Aid single blends vocals from several versions of the charity single that have been recorded over the years, so that George Michael duets with Harry Styles, and Chris Martin harmonises with the Sugababes.
Spandau Ballet singer Tony Hadley, who also sang on the original, told BBC Radio 2 that critics like Sheeran "should shut up, to be honest."
"If you take that route, then nobody does anything to help anybody. So it's just nonsense...
"Everybody's doing their bit to try and support various charities and we were doing our bit, innocently, to support what was happening in Ethiopia... So what do we do? Do we sit back and do nothing?"
'Identity crisis'
Speaking to the BBC Breakfast last month, Fuse ODG commented that while the original Band Aid project had been "touching" and well-intentioned, the lyrics and connected images were now having a damaging effect and stopping people from visiting Africa.
"It's been touching seeing the efforts that were put into it initially, the British public and different celebrities coming together to support a good cause, because there was a crisis at the time they needed attending to," he said.
"I have no problem with that, I think that was fantastic, and even just watching it back, I'm even getting emotional."
"But in that act of kindness, in that process of trying to help a crisis, we created another identity crisis," he continued.
"As a child who's now grown up in this era of images like that, Band Aid and initiatives like it have put Africa as a place of famine, a place of poverty, disease-filled.
"It took away our collective sense of pride and identity. So in the middle of trying to solve a temporary crisis, we've caused another dangerous crisis, which is an identity crisis for a whole continent."
He went on to tell BBC Africa that despite having been "excited" initially to be invited to take part in the latest rendtion of star-studded charity track, that his over-arching "mission" as an artist was to "realign how the world sees Africa and how Africans feel about themselves".
"It hit me that the images that the Band Aid project portrays just did not align with our mission to portray Africa in a positive light."
Speaking about the debate, Midge Ure recently acknowledged the criticisms of Band Aid's approach in the modern climate, saying it was "unfortunate" that Sheeran had not been contacted about the 2024 mix.
"I understand the whole thing about the 'white saviour complex'," he told Radio 2's Jeremy Vine. "It's not new. We've had this thrown at us for 40 years."
However, he said the song was not about portraying Africa in a negative light, but was trying to show the real-life consequences "of famine, of war, of conflict".
"And the result is children who need food, who need medication, who need education, and that's what we deal with."
Fuse ODG noted: "There's also starving children in the UK.”

a2725.t:
The first cross-border bus transportation service has officially been launched between the Kenyan and Ethiopian capitals, APA can report on Friday.
The ground service was launched this week by Abyssinia Luxury Coach, a transport company operating in the east African region. the company’s director Michael James Macchio, confirmed to local media.
Macchio said the launch introduces a direct bus connection between the two capital cities, filling a service gap left by previous operators.
The Ethiopian Ministry of Transport and Logistics in a statement disclosed on Thursday that it was not aware of the launch of bus public transport between Nairobi and Addis Ababa.
Citing the launch of the ground transportation by Abyssinia Luxury Coach, the ministry said it was done without its knowledge.
The ministry announced that while there was a national plan to start the service next Ethiopian fiscal year (2025/2026) fiscal year to create a connection between the two countries, the process requires a cooperation agreement, joint tariff setting, and other diplomatic issues between the two countries.
Prior to Abyssinia’s entry, Royal Allied, which was established four years ago, offered routes between Nairobi, Moyale, and Mombasa—but did not extend service beyond Moyale into Ethiopia.
MG/as/APA

a3413.t:
MONROVIA, LIBERIA-The Armed Forces of Liberia, in partnership with the US Government, has unveiled a new Tuberculosis Clinic at the 14th Military Hospital in Duazon, Margibi County.
The new clinic is expected to advance Liberia’s fight against tuberculosis in the military and civilian population.
According to a release issued recently, the clinic reaffirms the US Government’s longstanding commitment to support Liberia’s public health infrastructure.
The clinic highlights the broader collaboration between the United States and Liberia in preventive medicine to ensure that Liberia is equipped to handle public health emergencies.
The release added that the Tuberculosis Clinic will also be used to assist Liberians throughout the country as a central treatment center.
By: Frederick Teegwiah, Jr.

a3790.t:
The United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has appointed Coumba D. Sow of Senegal as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Togo, with the host Government’s approval, starting on 5 October.
Ms. Sow has 20 years of experience in development and humanitarian assistance. Previously she served as Representative for the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in Rwanda and in Djibouti, as FAO Coordinator of the Emergencies and Resilience for West Africa and the Sahel, and in other senior posts in the organization, including a position responsible for Africa in the Office of the FAO Director-General.
The report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of United Nations Secretary-General, stated that her experience also includes working on agricultural and rural development policies in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
It added that she holds a master’s degree in management of public policies from Sciences Po Paris, a postgraduate in agricultural economics at the University of London and Agroindustries in Montpellier.
GIK/APA

a4106.t:
In response to the devastating impact of Tropical Cyclone Chido, which struck northern Mozambique last December, the Mozambique LNG Project, operated by TotalEnergies, delivered past Tuesday, March 18, 2025, a humanitarian aid to the communities of Mecufi, in Cabo Delgado, in a partnership with the National Institute for Disaster Management (INGD) and the Diocesan Caritas of Pemba. The initiative will support over 600 families from 3 de Fevereiro, Capacira e Muaria.
During the ceremony, the General Manager of TotalEnergies, Maxime Rabilloud, stated: “we are here to express our solidarity with the families affected by Cyclone Chido on behalf of all Mozambique LNG Project partners and in reaction to the Government’s call to support the affected communities.”
The support includes food supplies for 627 families – 500 from the 3 de Fevereiro and 127 from the Capacira villages. Additionally, agricultural inputs will be distributed to 200 families in Muaria village, while construction materials will be provided to an equal number of families in critical need in the 3 de Fevereiro village.
On his turn, the Governor of Cabo Delgado, Valige Tauabo, recognized TotalEnergies efforts for its ongoing commitment to disaster relief and humanitarian assistance.
“We recognize that this support alone will not solve all the challenges caused by Cyclone Chido. That is why we continue to mobilize additional resources. In the meantime, we encourage the population to rebuild their homes and strengthen agricultural production to ensure food security and income generation”- said the Governor.
With more than 100,000 people affected, humanitarian efforts are now focused on distributing essential goods in the hardest-hit districts of Pemba and Mecufi, ensuring immediate relief and supporting long-term recovery.
The Mozambique LNG Project’s support reflects its commitment to sustainable development and improvement of the quality of life in the region.

a4472.t:
In a bid to strengthen Malawi’s democratic institutions, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Malawi, in collaboration with other development partners, has committed $8.3 million (approximately K14.5 billion) for the September 16 General Elections.
UNDP Malawi Resident Representative Fenella Frost confirmed the development yesterday.
She said the Malawi Electoral Support Project (MESP) Basket Fund initiative, which is running from 2023 to 2025, is designed to bolster the country’s electoral processes, ensuring free, fair and credible elections.
“The partners include the European Union (EU), the United States Agency for International Development (USaid), the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), the Royal Norwegian Embassy and the Embassy of Ireland,” Frost said.
On his part, European Union (EU) Ambassador to Malawi Rune Skinnebach said the EU and partners reaffirmed their commitment to supporting Malawi’s electoral process through their contribution to the election basket fund.
- Advertisement -
He said, as in previous elections, the bloc remains the largest donor to the basket fund, which is financing several activities in support of the electoral process.
“The EU is the biggest donor in the basket fund, which is doing a number of activities to support the elections.
“However, the elections are primarily funded by the government, and the Malawi Electoral Commission has been assured that, once again, appropriate government funding will be made available, ensuring the smooth organisation of the polls,” Skinnebach said.
Beyond funding, the EU is also supporting key institutions such as the Ministry of Local Government and the National Registration Bureau in preparation for the elections.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
Additionally, the EU will provide training for media professionals after the elections, as well as offer support to the Malawi Police Service in areas related to election security.
The EU will also be involved in election observation, with an exploratory mission set to arrive at the end of the month to assess the feasibility of a full-fledged EU Electoral Monitoring Mission.
“I expect the mission will confirm the feasibility, and then we will deploy a large EU election monitoring team a few months before the elections to assess and document the electoral process,” the ambassador said.

a4804.t:
Kampala, Uganda | THE INDEPENDENT | Acholi Sub-region has registered a reduction in new cases of HIV/Aids infections.
A new report reveals that new cases of HIV/Aids in the region had lowered by 72 percent from 11,358 in 2017 to just 3,175 in 2021.
This was disclosed during the second Regional Health Assembly held in Gulu City on Thursday.
Presenting the regional HIV prevalence report, Peter Erem, the Director of Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning at The Aids Support Organization-TASO says new cases of HIV being diagnosed had reduced significantly in the last four years.
He also noted that the region has registered a reduction in the prevalence at 7.4 percent in 2021, a 15 percent from 8.7 percent in 2017. The National HIV prevalence stood at 5.3 percent by 2021, a reduction of 6.0 percent in 2017.
Erem’s report also indicates that HIV cases are higher among females at 9.3 percent compared to 5.3 percent among males in the region.
According to Erem, whereas the region has achieved the 95 percent targets of HIV patients being on ART treatment and knowing their status, the challenge remains on viral load suppression among adults and children.
The report indicates that only 84 percent of viral load suppression had been achieved for all ages but was much lower among children under 14 years old.
The Mid North has the fourth highest HIV prevalence of 7.6 percent and the Acholi Sub-region in particular still has lower than optimal viral load suppression for people living with HIV, especially children.
During the same assembly, USAID Regional Health Integration to Enhance Services in North, Acholi-RHITES-N launched the five years Government to Government (G2G) activity in Gulu Regional Referral Hospital.
At least 2.6 billion shillings have been earmarked for the implementation of the first year of the project starting in the Financial Year 2022/2023.
Dr. Peter Mukobi, the Director of Gulu Regional Referral Hospital says the project will be helpful for the community in improving access to services. He says the project seeks to improve services in the areas of maternal, and neonatal child health, HIV, TB, and Nutrition citing that it will be a big boost for the facility.
Dr. Abel Nkolo, the Chief of Party USAID RHITES-N in Acholi noted that they are grateful for their continued partnerships with the district authorities in addressing health concerns in the region.
“We hope to continue to work together to improve overall health in Acholi Sub-region,” He said.
Chris Mugarura the Assistant Commissioner in charge of the Health Policy and Sector Planning Division at the Health Ministry lauded the planners of the health assembly saying it’s an avenue to enlist the help of decision-makers and funders in order to improve access to healthcare.
Mugarura however says whereas the country has made great strides in bringing services nearer to the people, the quality still remains low arguing that there is a need to shift focus on sharing knowledge on evidence-based strategies.
The second Annual Regional Health Assembly convened under the theme “Invigorating Health Promotion and Disease Prevention: My Role, Your Role, Our Role” attracted over 100 leaders in various capacities from Acholi Sub-region.
*****
URN

a5020.t:
As I traverse the various parts of our beloved Western Region—from Half-Assini to Elubo to Tarkwa to Sekondi-Takoradi, Amenfi West to Amenfi East and virtually every corner of the region, I am confronted with a sobering truth: our once-thriving region has been reduced to a shadow of its former self under the Akufo-Addo-Bawumia-led New Patriotic Party (NPP) government.
The stark reality is that, under their leadership, the Western Region has languished, its development stunted , and its people left to grapple with neglect.
The Empty Promises of the NPP
The litany of unfulfilled promises made by the NPP is both alarming and disheartening.
The NPP government, in its bid to secure our votes, made grand declarations about transforming our region into an oil services hub with world-class port facilities.
They pledged to construct a new regional hospital, rehabilitate the Effia-Nkwanta Hospital, and modernize the Takoradi Port.
They spoke of establishing an Accident and Emergency Centre in Takoradi and an oil refinery in Sekondi-Takoradi.
Yet, these promises remain largely unfulfilled, leaving our roads, healthcare system and infrastructure in a state of disrepair.
The Aggressive Rural Electrification Program we embarked on in the region during my tenure as Minister of Energy was truncated, leaving many communities in the region struggling to access electricity in this modern age.
The NDC: A Proven Blueprint for Progress
In stark contrast, the National Democratic Congress (NDC) and former President John Mahama have a demonstrated commitment to prioritizing the development of the Western Region.
As H.E John Mahama aptly stated, “The Western Region is one of the most important regions in this country because of its enormous contribution to the advancement of Ghana.”
This acknowledgment is reflected in the significant achievements during his administration, which include:
The developmental projects of the erstwhile NDC administration in the region include but not limited to the following:
- Takoradi Port Expansion: Under Mahama’s leadership, significant expansions were made to the Takoradi Port, enhancing its capacity to facilitate trade and commerce.
- Atuabo Gas Processing Plant: The establishment of this facility has been a game-changer for the energy sector, providing gas for power generation and industrial use.
- ENI Onshore Receiving Facility at Sanzule: This facility has improved the management of gas resources and contributed to the region’s economic growth.
- Quantum LPG Terminal PLC:
A private sector led initiative has helped to curtail the LPG line in Ghana and reduced our country’s LPG imports by 50%
- Sekondi Fishing Harbour Phase 2. This project has greatly improved the fishing industry’s infrastructure, benefiting local fishermen and the economy.
- Sekondi-Takoradi-KojoKrom Railway Lines: The revival and expansion of railway services have improved transportation and connectivity in the region.
- Construction of Multiple Community High Schools: Schools such as Sankor Community High School, Gwiraman Community High School, Samraboi Community Day School, and Manso Amenfi Community Day School were built, enhancing educational opportunities for our youth.
- Tarkwa-BOGOSO-Anyanfuri Road: This vital road project improved transportation and access to markets for communities along the route.
- Apimnim to Elubo International Road: The upgrading of this international road has facilitated trade and movement between Ghana and neighboring countries.
- Takoradi Library Complex: This facility has provided a valuable resource for education and community engagement.
- Tarkwa Government Hospital: The hospital was expanded and upgraded to better serve the healthcare needs of the community.
- Doctors and Nurses Flat / 120 Bed Takoradi Hospital Project: Although this project faced challenges and was abandoned, it reflects the ambitious plans of the past administration to improve healthcare infrastructure.
- Sekondi Youth Center: This center has provided a space for youth development and engagement.
- Teachers Resource Center (Sekondi): This facility has supported the professional development of educators in the region.
- Industrial Drive: Through government facilitation and support several factories were established, but including Diamond Cement Factory, Twyfood Ceramics Factory, Karma Distilleries Factory, and others, created jobs and stimulated the local economy.
- Cold Stores at Shama, New Takoradi, and Half Assini: These facilities have supported the fishing and agricultural industries by reducing post-harvest losses.
- Upgrading of the Bogoso Health Center to Policlinic under Euroject Project: This upgrade has improved healthcare delivery in the Bogoso area.
- Extension of Ghana Gas to Prestea: This project powered mining companies in the enclave, boosting local economic activity.
- Equipping the Effia Nkwanta Regional Hospital: The introduction of modern medical equipment, including MRI scanners, has improved healthcare services in the region.
A Disgraceful Disregard for Our Heroes
To compound our challenges, the current government has not only failed to deliver on its promises but has also shown a complete disregard for our heroes.
The derogatory language directed at Osagyefo Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, a son of the soil, is a direct affront to our identity and history.
Nkrumah envisioned a prosperous Ghana that included a thriving Western Region, yet we find ourselves at a crossroads, with our voices muted and our contributions overlooked.
H.E John Dramani Mahama has promised to restore our founder and first president of Ghana his rightful place in our country’s history.
Furthermore, the absence of any Western Region native in the current cabinet underscores the systemic sidelining of our people.
How can we expect to have a key voice in the executive government when our own are excluded from the decision-making table?
This lack of representation is not just a political oversight; it is a deliberate strategy that perpetuates our marginalization.
For far too long, we have been sidelined while other regions flourish.
We must reclaim our rightful place in the national discourse and demand the development and respect we deserve.
I urge every citizen of the Western Region to reflect on the implications of our current leadership.
The NPP has failed us, reneging on their promises and leaving us to fend for ourselves.
The NDC, under the leadership of John Mahama, offers a renewed focus on the development of our region.
We can expect a government that recognizes our contributions to the national economy and is committed to fostering an environment where we can thrive.
Let us come together and raise our voices in unison.
We possess the power to effect change, and it begins with our vote. When we cast our ballots for John Mahama and the NDC, we are voting for a future where the Western Region is no longer overlooked but is celebrated for its potential and contributions.
The time for action is now. Let us rise to the occasion and ensure that our beloved Western Region is counted among the leaders of development in Ghana. Vote for John Mahama and the NDC—a choice for progress, respect, and a brighter future for all of us.
Together, we can turn the tide and usher in a new era of development and prosperity for the Western Region.
Our voices matter, and our future is in our hands.
Let us choose wisely for the sake of our children and generations to come.
Together, we can transform our cherished region into a more befitting status.
JOHN MAHAMA AND NDC WILL DEVELOP WESTERN REGION AGAIN.
Western Region Deserves Better.
Hon.Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah
(Deputy Majority Leader and MP for ELLEMBELLE constituency)

a5103.t:
Pourquoi les États-Unis peinent à maintenir leur crédibilité en Afrique ?
En août, l’armée américaine a fermé sa dernière base militaire au Niger, déclarée « illégale » selon un accord de coopération militaire entre les deux pays. En mai, l’Éthiopie a qualifié de « conseil non sollicité » l’intervention de l’ambassadeur américain sur ses affaires intérieures.
Ces exemples reflètent un mécontentement plus large des pays africains envers les États-Unis, un sentiment qui dépasse les incidents isolés. La crédibilité de Washington se dégrade, comme en témoigne la baisse de l’image positive du leadership américain sur le continent.
D’après un sondage Gallup sur la perception du leadership mondial, le taux d’approbation médian des États-Unis en Afrique est passé de 59 % en 2022 à 56 % en 2023. Parmi les principales puissances mondiales, les États-Unis sont les seuls à n’avoir pas vu leur image s’améliorer en Afrique cette année.
Bien que les États-Unis aient joué un rôle central dans les affaires africaines, leur déficit de crédibilité persiste et pourrait même s’aggraver dans certains cas.
Promesses non tenues
Depuis le premier sommet États-Unis-Afrique sous Obama en 2014, les pays africains espéraient davantage d’investissements américains. Cependant, au lieu d’une augmentation, les échanges commerciaux entre les États-Unis et l’Afrique ont fortement diminué.
Selon le Bureau du recensement des États-Unis, les échanges sont passés de 113 milliards de dollars en 2010 à 67,4 milliards en 2023. De même, les investissements directs étrangers (IDE) en Afrique, qui avaient atteint un sommet de 69 milliards de dollars en 2014, ont chuté à 44,81 milliards en 2020, pour ensuite remonter à 56,29 milliards en 2023.
Le programme « Prospective Afrique », lancé par le gouvernement de Trump en 2018 pour dynamiser la croissance via le commerce et l’investissement, n’a pas donné les résultats escomptés. De plus, Trump, qui n’a jamais visité le continent, a réduit le budget de l’Agence américaine pour le développement international (USAID). L’aide américaine est souvent conditionnée à des questions de droits de l’homme, ajoutant à l’incertitude.
Cameron Hudson, Senior Fellow au Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), souligne que ce manque de résultats, combiné à des promesses excessives, n’a fait que renforcer l’image de Washington comme un partenaire peu fiable et hypocrite.
Arrogance et déconnexion des réalités africaines
Un épisode marquant du sommet États-Unis-Afrique de 2022 a fait grand bruit : plus de 50 dirigeants africains ont été transportés en bus vers le lieu de la rencontre, un geste jugé irrespectueux. Le président kényan, William Ruto, s’est indigné de ce traitement, déclarant qu’il était inapproprié de « nous entasser dans des bus comme des écoliers ».
Arikana Chihombori-Quao, ancienne représentante de l’Union africaine aux États-Unis, a ajouté que ce manque de respect illustre l’attitude historique des États-Unis envers l’Afrique. L’approche américaine est souvent perçue comme déconnectée des réalités africaines.
Aussi, le politologue bissau-guinéen Seco Cassama estime que les États-Unis imposent leurs intérêts sans tenir compte des traditions et des civilisations africaines. Il cite l’exemple de la présence militaire américaine au Niger, où, malgré l’ouverture de la base aérienne 201 à Agadez en 2018, les attaques terroristes ont continué d’augmenter, soulignant l’inefficacité des stratégies américaines.
Ingérence et imposition
En septembre, trois Américains impliqués dans une tentative de coup d’État en République démocratique du Congo ont été condamnés à mort, un autre exemple de l’ingérence américaine dans les affaires africaines.
Lors de la visite de la vice-présidente Kamala Harris en mars 2023, Fred M’membe, président du Parti socialiste de Zambie, a critiqué les États-Unis pour leur ingérence historique en Afrique, tout en s’érigeant aujourd’hui en promoteurs de la démocratie. Les projets américains en Afrique, comme l’AGOA (Africa Growth and Opportunity Act), sont souvent conditionnés à des critères non économiques tels que la protection des droits de l’homme et la démocratie.
Le Gabon, le Niger, l’Ouganda et la République centrafricaine, par exemple, seront exclus de l’AGOA en janvier 2024 en raison de préoccupations liées aux droits de l’homme. Selon le journal zimbabwéen Herald, cette attitude américaine, combinée à son pouvoir économique, est perçue comme une forme d’arrogance qui alimente le ressentiment en Afrique.

a5103.en:
Why are the United States struggling to maintain their credibility in Africa?

In August, the American army closed its last military base in Niger, declared "illegal" under a military cooperation agreement between the two countries. In May, Ethiopia described the US ambassador's intervention in its internal affairs as "unsolicited advice."

These examples reflect a broader discontent among African countries towards the United States, a sentiment that goes beyond isolated incidents. Washington's credibility is deteriorating, as shown by the decline in the positive image of American leadership on the continent.

According to a Gallup poll on the perception of global leadership, the median approval rating of the United States in Africa fell from 59% in 2022 to 56% in 2023. Among the world's major powers, the United States is the only one whose image in Africa did not improve this year.

Although the United States has played a central role in African affairs, its credibility deficit persists and could even worsen in some cases.

Unkept promises

Since the first US-Africa summit under Obama in 2014, African countries had hoped for more American investment. However, instead of an increase, trade between the United States and Africa has sharply declined.

According to the US Census Bureau, trade fell from 113 billion dollars in 2010 to 67.4 billion in 2023. Likewise, foreign direct investment (FDI) in Africa, which had reached a peak of 69 billion dollars in 2014, fell to 44.81 billion in 2020, before rising again to 56.29 billion in 2023.

The "Prosper Africa" program, launched by the Trump administration in 2018 to boost growth through trade and investment, did not produce the expected results. Moreover, Trump, who never visited the continent, cut the budget of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). American aid is often conditioned on human rights issues, adding to the uncertainty.

Cameron Hudson, Senior Fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), stresses that this lack of results, combined with excessive promises, has only reinforced Washington's image as an unreliable and hypocritical partner.

Arrogance and disconnection from African realities

One striking episode from the 2022 US-Africa summit caused a stir: more than 50 African leaders were transported by bus to the meeting venue, a gesture seen as disrespectful. Kenyan President William Ruto was indignant at this treatment, declaring that it was inappropriate to "cram us into buses like schoolchildren."

Arikana Chihombori-Quao, former African Union representative to the United States, added that this lack of respect illustrates the historical attitude of the United States towards Africa. The American approach is often perceived as disconnected from African realities.

Likewise, the Bissau-Guinean political scientist Seco Cassama believes that the United States imposes its interests without taking African traditions and civilizations into account. He cites the example of the American military presence in Niger, where, despite the opening of Air Base 201 in Agadez in 2018, terrorist attacks have continued to increase, underlining the ineffectiveness of American strategies.

Interference and imposition

In September, three Americans involved in an attempted coup d'état in the Democratic Republic of Congo were sentenced to death, another example of American interference in African affairs.

During Vice President Kamala Harris's visit in March 2023, Fred M'membe, president of the Socialist Party of Zambia, criticized the United States for its historical interference in Africa while today setting itself up as a promoter of democracy. American projects in Africa, such as AGOA (Africa Growth and Opportunity Act), are often conditioned on non-economic criteria such as the protection of human rights and democracy.

Gabon, Niger, Uganda and the Central African Republic, for example, will be excluded from AGOA in January 2024 because of human rights concerns. According to the Zimbabwean newspaper The Herald, this American attitude, combined with its economic power, is perceived as a form of arrogance that fuels resentment in Africa.
